title: Implementation of Code of Good Practice for Milk Producers in the dairy industry

lessons.title: Assessing the farm against the code
lessons.html:
From knowing the code to living it

In this work experience module you will help put the Code of Good Practice for milk producers into practice on a working dairy. You will check the farm against the code, help fix gaps and keep evidence in your logbook and portfolio.

Step 1: a self-assessment

Use a checklist based on the code and the milk buyer's requirements. Walk the farm with the manager and score each area: complies, partly complies, does not comply.

AreaQuestions to ask
Milk hygieneIs the full routine followed? Are cleaning and tank temperature records complete?
MedicinesAre treated cows marked? Are withdrawal dates recorded? Is the medicine store locked and tidy?
Animal welfareAre cows calm, in good condition, not lame? Is there shade, water and clean lying space?
Feed and waterIs feed stored safely and free of mould? Are suppliers recorded? Is water clean?
EnvironmentIs effluent contained? Are chemicals stored safely and empty containers disposed of correctly?
PeopleAre workers trained, given protective equipment and treated fairly?

Step 2: collect evidence

For each area, gather proof: records, photos, training registers, vet reports. An auditor will ask, "Show me."

Step 3: list the gaps

Write down every gap clearly, for example: "Treatment board not updated on weekends" or "Empty detergent drums stored next to the calf feed." Rank the gaps by risk. Anything that could put residues in milk or harm people or animals is high priority.

Include workers in the walk-through. Ask milkers, calf rearers and feeders how they do their tasks. Their answers often reveal gaps that records do not show, such as a step skipped on night shifts or a missing piece of equipment.

lessons.title: Planning and carrying out improvements
lessons.html:
The action plan

Turn the list of gaps into an action plan. For each gap record:

  • What will be done.
  • Who is responsible.
  • By when.
  • What it will cost, if anything.
  • How you will know it is fixed.

Example action plan

GapActionWho / when
Treatment board not updated on weekendsAdd treatment board check to weekend relief milker's shift checklist; train relief milkersSupervisor, this week
Empty chemical drums near calf feedMove to a marked, fenced area for collection by the supplier or approved disposalStores worker, today
No written calf protocolWrite protocol with the vet; display in calf shedManager and vet, this month
Some cows lameHoof trimmer visit, repair track near gate, footbath as vet advisesManager, next two weeks

Writing standard operating procedures

Many gaps happen because workers do things differently. A short standard operating procedure (SOP) helps. Keep it to one page, use numbered steps and simple words, translate it into the languages your team speaks, and put it up where the job is done, for example the milking routine on the parlour wall.

Training the team

Train workers on each new SOP. Show, let them practise, check them, and record who was trained and when. Explain the reason: a residue can cost the farm a tanker of milk; a lame cow suffers and gives less milk.

The legal base

Remember that many code requirements come from law, including the Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962, the Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984, Act 36 of 1947, the National Water Act 36 of 1998 and the OHS Act 85 of 1993.

lessons.title: Monitoring and keeping standards up
lessons.html:
Making improvements stick

Standards slip when nobody checks. Build monitoring into normal work.

Monitoring tools

  • Daily checklists for milking, calf unit and feeding, signed by the person on duty.
  • Weekly supervisor walk-through using the code checklist.
  • Monthly review of buyer results (bacteria, SCC, residues), calf deaths, lameness scores and incidents.
  • Repeat self-assessment before the buyer's audit and at least yearly.

Measuring progress

Choose a few measures and track them on a board in the office, for example average SCC, number of clinical mastitis cases, calf deaths per 100 calves born, number of residue incidents (target zero) and lame cows per 100 cows. Share the trends with the team.

Handling a non-conformance

If an audit or a test finds a problem:

  1. Contain it: for example, divert or dump affected milk.
  2. Investigate the root cause by asking why several times.
  3. Correct it and prevent recurrence with an SOP change or training.
  4. Record and report to the buyer if required.
  5. Check that the fix works over the next weeks.

Building a culture

The code works best when every worker sees it as "how we do things here", not as extra paperwork. Praise good practice, involve workers in solving problems, and make sure managers follow the same rules.

Key points

  • Start with a self-assessment against the code and the buyer's requirements.
  • Rank gaps by risk and fix residue and safety risks first.
  • Use an action plan with responsibilities and dates.
  • Write simple SOPs and train workers on them.
  • Monitor with checklists, walk-throughs and monthly reviews.
